blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — spironolactone/ACE-inhibitor/potassium interaction teaching
stem: A client takes spironolactone and an ACE inhibitor and reports using a potassium-containing salt substitute every day. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.A: Continue the potassium-containing salt substitute because it does not materially affect serum potassium when spironolactone is combined with an ACE inhibitor.
options.B: Avoid adding the potassium-containing salt substitute without prescriber review because spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor can increase hyperkalemia risk.
options.C: Use the potassium-containing salt substitute to offset expected potassium loss because spironolactone and ACE inhibitors both lower serum potassium.
options.D: Increase potassium-rich foods together with the salt substitute because potassium depletion is the principal electrolyte concern with this medication combination.

rationale: Current spironolactone prescribing information warns that spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia and that the risk is increased by potassium supplementation, potassium-containing salt substitutes, and drugs that increase potassium, including ACE inhibitors. The label directs serum-potassium monitoring and notes that concomitant agents that raise potassium can lead to severe hyperkalemia. Therefore B is the best answer. A incorrectly dismisses the effect of the salt substitute, while C and D reverse the potassium risk by treating depletion as the expected problem.
educational_objective: Teach clients taking spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor to avoid unreviewed potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes because the combination can increase hyperkalemia risk and requires serum-potassium monitoring.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine); Rising Pharma Holdings, Inc.
source_document_title: Spironolactone Tablets, for oral use — Prescribing Information
source_version_date: Revised March 2026; current DailyMed label accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Full Prescribing Information §5.1 Hyperkalemia: spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia; risk is increased by potassium supplementation, potassium-containing salt substitutes, and drugs that increase potassium such as ACE inhibitors and ARBs; monitor serum potassium after initiation/titration and regularly thereafter. §7.1 Drugs and Supplements Increasing Serum Potassium: concomitant potassium supplementation or potassium-raising drugs may lead to severe hyperkalemia; ACE inhibitors are listed among drugs that can increase potassium.
source_claim_supported: Spironolactone combined with an ACE inhibitor and a potassium-containing salt substitute increases hyperkalemia risk and warrants potassium-safety review and monitoring.
blueprint_locator: Printed p. 38, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: review pertinent data before medication administration, including contraindications and potential interactions; educate clients about medications; evaluate client response to medication; handle and administer high-risk medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rebuilt all four alternatives as parallel client-teaching statements of comparable length rather than electrolyte labels with one explanatory long answer.
Placed the correct response in a nonterminal option and removed the uniquely longest-answer pattern.
Kept the construct on the exact labeled interaction among spironolactone, ACE inhibition, and potassium-containing salt substitutes without adding unsupported thresholds.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms B uniquely matches §§5.1 and 7.1. A incorrectly dismisses a labeled potassium source, while C and D reverse the expected electrolyte direction. The item contains no unsupported numeric threshold, no second defensible answer, and no material length or absolute-word cue.
